chunks: From him, from al-Qasim, from Ali, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Regarding the fingers, for each finger is ten camels.
Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: These narrations are agreed upon, not differing.

And Zarif ibn Nasih has narrated in his narration that the fingers are equal except for the thumb, for it has a separate blood money, and it is that it has one-third of the hand's blood money, and two-thirds of the blood money between the four fingers equally.
And we have cited his narration in its form in our book, Al-Kabir.
And it is permissible to reconcile these narrations with this distinction.

As for what the narration of Abu Basir and Abdillah ibn Sinan included, that in each finger is ten camels, it is permissible that it be from the speech of the narrator, namely that when he heard that the fingers are equal in blood money, he interpreted it as ten camels for each finger, and he did not know that this ruling is specific to the four fingers.
And we said this so that the action may be based on all the narrations without discarding any of them.

key_terms.إِبِل: Camels (traditional unit of currency in Islamic law)
key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money or compensation for injury/death

ai.seo_question: What is the blood money for each finger according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In *Al-Istibsar*, Shaykh al-Tusi highlights the principle of *jam'* (reconciliation) between seemingly contradictory reports regarding finger *diyah*, specifically resolving the discrepancy between a uniform ten-camel valuation and the distinct status of the thumb. This scholarly approach preserves the authority of all narrations by interpreting the 'ten camels' figure as a narrator's explanatory gloss rather than a rigid legal definition, thereby ensuring practical consistency in Shia jurisprudence.
